answer.rationale: Renegotiating at this renewal is the only direction that can pursue the 18% cost mandate without adding delivery risk. memory_c1 (incumbent integration stayed stable across cycles) and memory_c4 (benchmarking at renewal moved the incumbent on price and payment terms) support negotiating rather than merely renewing; memory_c6 suggests a longer-term/volume lever is available if price alone stalls. Switching the primary vendor (memory_c2) is rejected at 94% utilization with zero buffer — it increases delivery risk regardless of historical onboarding success. Adding a second source (memory_c3) hedges risk but doesn't cut spend. Deferral (memory_c5) is unsafe here because this contract explicitly does not auto-renew, so deferral risks a supply gap. Residual risk flagged: the incumbent may not concede the full 18%, and talks must conclude before the 14-day expiry; a month-to-month bridge or staged switch remains the fallback next cycle. Optionality to switch or dual-source later is preserved. Verified memory_c4 because it is the load-bearing claim — that renewal renegotiation with this incumbent has actually yielded margin before.
